did_you_know.text: The Lord compares pouring out His Spirit on Israel to pouring water on thirsty, parched ground; the water and blessing symbolize life, growth, and renewal.

The verse describes several ways a person expresses belonging to the Lord: saying, “I belong to the Lord,” being called by the name of Jacob, writing on his hand that he belongs to the Lord, and calling himself by the name of Israel.
The Lord presents Himself as the “First” and the “Last,” emphasizing that there is no God besides Him. This is a central expression of His uniqueness and exclusivity.

Israel is called to be a witness to the truth about the Lord and not to be afraid. The question, “Is there any god besides Me?” reinforces the claim that there is no other rock or true deity besides Him.
The prophet emphasizes that the material from which a person makes an idol is a natural substance intended primarily for human needs; the tree grows through the rain and is cut down by human hands.
The same tree is used for warmth, baking bread, and roasting meat, but from what remains, the person makes an idol. This contrast exposes the contradiction at the heart of idolatry.
The idol worshiper is described as one who “feeds on ashes,” meaning that he clings to something worthless and fails to recognize that the idol in his hand is a lie and cannot save him.

The Lord describes the forgiveness of sins as something erased and made to disappear: “I have wiped away your transgressions like a cloud.” He then calls Israel to return to Him, because He has redeemed them.
The joy over Israel’s redemption is not limited to human beings: the heavens, the earth, the mountains, the forest, and every tree in it are all called to sing and share in the joy of redemption.
At the end of the chapter, Cyrus is mentioned by name as the one whom the Lord calls “My shepherd” and to whom He assigns a role in rebuilding Jerusalem and laying the foundations of the Temple.
